A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CauIM study despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. The supplied v2 ends at the references; v3 additionally contains Appendices A–I, which were included in the comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original diffusion experiments on four datasets, including influence scores, runtimes, and noise and propagation-probability sensitivity results.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original experimental results on four datasets. Appendix Figure 5 additionally reports individual-ITE distributions for GoodReads and Contact.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 adds parameter adjustment to keep estimated ITEs bounded during propagation. A-CauIM replaces simulated binary activations with a differentiable probability transformation for estimating expected ITEs. Equation 5 also changes seed selection from the derivative alone to the derivative multiplied by activation probability. These alter the procedure substantially.

E1.justification: Both versions use GoodReads, Contact, Email-Eu and SD-100 for the same influence-maximization task. The expanded scenario descriptions and new distribution plots concern these retained datasets, without establishing additional task or population coverage.

E2.justification: The reported comparisons retain Traditional Greedy and Random alongside G-CauIM and A-CauIM. V3 further describes the greedy baseline as lacking parameter adjustment, without establishing a changed comparator procedure. CELF-CauIM and HDD-CauIM receive appendix pseudocode but no reported comparative evaluation.

E3.justification: The timing comparison changes its stated environment from CPU in v2 Table 1 to GPU in v3 Table 2. This is a reported evaluation-setting revision; the PDFs do not establish whether timings were rerun. The seed budget of 15, propagation probability of 0.01, influence metric and 20 influence-estimation rounds remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V3 Figure 5 adds a descriptive analysis of individual-ITE distributions in GoodReads and Contact. The existing noise and propagation-probability sensitivity analyses are retained and regrouped in Figure 3; no new component-ablation comparison is reported.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 10 repetitions and report the same variance-versus-noise curves. Appendix C.3 clarifies aggregation across those realizations without establishing additional runs or a changed uncertainty-reporting practice. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: The baseline runtime row changes across all four datasets: for example, GoodReads changes from 89 seconds to one day and Email-Eu from 1029 seconds to 22 hours. This substantially changes the reported efficiency comparison, although the CPU-to-GPU caption change prevents a same-setting interpretation. Other runtime rows and all main influence scores are identical. V3 also adds ITE-distribution results.

T1.justification: The main guarantee and robustness statements are retained, but Appendices D and F–H add a set-cover hardness argument and detailed derivations where v2 provides sketches or unresolved appendix references. Equation 2 changes the cardinality constraint from exactly K to at most K and explicitly averages over activation states. Section 3 also revises the complexity accounting.

C1.justification: The central claims about causal node gains, approximate guarantees, robustness and acceleration remain. However, v2's conclusion asserts seamless extension to other classic IM algorithms, whereas v3 treats difficulties with sketch-based extensions as future work, qualifying the broader transferability claim.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations of soft treatments and probability-weighted derivatives through differentiability and local perturbations. Section 7 changes the stated sparse-graph concern for sketch methods from failure to reach the theoretical optimum to reduced efficiency. Appendix I additionally discusses why locally high neighboring ITE need not yield globally influential seeds.

D1.justification: V3 supplies substantial previously unavailable documentation: Gaussian-mixture covariate parameters, initial-treatment generation, an HGCN update, training details and auxiliary pseudocode. Section 5 adds an implementation-code link. The environment changes from Python 3.8 to 3.10.14; Appendix C.3 reports Torch 2.1, conflicting with Table 2's Torch 1.11.0.

R1.justification: V3 adds supporting works including Ma and Tresp, Harshaw et al., and Mossel and Roch, while removing works such as Li and Wager. Appendices B and I expand comparisons with weighted, heuristic and sketch-based IM. The central positioning around dynamic causal gains remains intact.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper, changes the author line, and extensively rewrites the introduction, preliminaries and methodology. It reorganizes the challenges and algorithm descriptions, condenses overlapping causal-inference background, and distributes supporting material across named appendices. Many unresolved appendix references are replaced with concrete destinations.

P2.justification: V3 adds a motivation diagram, redraws algorithm diagrams, and moves the propagation illustration and G-CauIM diagram into appendices. V2 Figures 4–5 become a smaller four-panel Figure 3. New ITE-distribution plots and conceptual comparison Tables 3–4 further change the visual presentation substantially.

improvement.justification: V3 improves assessability by supplying derivations, algorithm details and data-generation instructions that v2 leaves behind unresolved appendix references. Its revised framing also clarifies environmental sensitivity. However, unchanged influence results provide no distinct validation of the revised algorithm steps, and conflicting runtime-environment descriptions weaken reproducibility. These limitations temper the documentation gains and prevent a confident judgment of substantial overall improvement.
